{{Confusing|date=November 2022}}

'''Reciprocity''' in [[linear system]]s is the principle that a response '''Rab''', measured at a location (and direction if applicable) '''a''', when the system has an excitation signal applied at a location (and direction if applicable) '''b''', is exactly equal to '''Rba''' which is the response at location '''b''', when that same excitation is applied at '''a'''. This applies for all frequencies of the excitation signal. If '''Hab''' is the [[transfer function]] between '''a''' and '''b''' then '''Hab'''&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''Hba''', if the system is linear.

In the special case of a [[modal analysis]] this is known as Maxwell's reciprocity theorem.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Experimental modal analysis | url=http://www.sdrl.uc.edu/academic-course-info/academic-course-info/docs/ucme663/v3_1.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907003439/http://www.sdrl.uc.edu/academic-course-info/academic-course-info/docs/ucme663/v3_1.pdf | archive-date=2008-09-07}}</ref>  In electromagnetism the concept is known as [[Reciprocity (electromagnetism)|Lorentz reciprocity]], a special case of which is the [[Reciprocity (electrical networks)|reciprocity theorem]] of electrical networks.

The reciprocity principle is also used in the analysis of structures.<ref>{{Cite book | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=FEQ0H3o-lfoC&dq=reciprocity+load+deflection&pg=PA339 | title = Mechanical Vibration: Analysis, Uncertainties, and Control | isbn = 9780824753801 | last1 = Benaroya | first1 = Haym | year = 2004| publisher = CRC Press }}</ref> When combined with [[Superposition principle|superposition]], symmetry and anti-symmetry, it can be used to resolve complex load conditions.
